lead: The inverse Z-transform recovers the sequence x[n] from its z-domain expression X(z). The algebra alone is not enough: the region of convergence (ROC) fixes whether each pole produces a right-sided or a left-sided term. The formal inverse is a contour integral, but three practical methods do the work: power series, partial fractions and residues. Engineers use it to turn a transfer function or a difference-equation solution back into a discrete-time signal, for example the samples of a speech frame or the impulse response of a digital filter.
prereq: You need: chapter 6.4 for X(z) and the ROC, chapter 6.5 for standard pairs, and Unit 4, Inverse Laplace transform by partial fractions, for the algebra.

sections.h3: The inversion formula and what the ROC does

blocks.text: The formal inverse is a contour integral. Evaluate it inside the ROC, not on a pole.

blocks.where: C is a closed counterclockwise contour inside the ROC; j = √(−1); n is the sample index; X(z) is the z-transform.

blocks.text: Direct integration is rare. Power series, or long division, is the first practical method. If the ROC is |z| > r, the sequence is right-sided, so divide to get a series in z⁻¹: X(z) = Σ x[n] z<sup>−n</sup>. Read x[n] as the coefficient of z<sup>−n</sup>. If the ROC is |z| < r, the sequence is left-sided, so divide to get a series in positive powers of z: X(z) = Σ x[−m] z<sup>m</sup>. Read x[−m] as the coefficient of z<sup>m</sup>. Partial fractions and residues are the other two methods.

sections.h3: Partial fractions: split X(z)/z and let the ROC choose the side

blocks.text: Partial fractions turn X(z) into first-order terms whose inverse pairs are known. The ROC decides the side of each term.

items: Factor the denominator of X(z) to find the poles p<sub>k</sub>.
Form X(z)/z and write it as Σ A<sub>k</sub>/(z − p<sub>k</sub>).
Find each coefficient from A<sub>k</sub> = (z − p<sub>k</sub>) X(z)/z evaluated at z = p<sub>k</sub>.
Multiply back by z: X(z) = Σ A<sub>k</sub> z/(z − p<sub>k</sub>) = Σ A<sub>k</sub>/(1 − p<sub>k</sub> z<sup>−1</sup>).
Use the ROC of each pole: |z| > |p<sub>k</sub>| gives p<sub>k</sub><sup>n</sup>u[n]; |z| < |p<sub>k</sub>| gives −p<sub>k</sub><sup>n</sup>u[−n−1].

blocks.text: The same term 1/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹) gives 0.5ⁿu[n] when |z| > 0.5, and −0.5ⁿu[−n−1] when |z| < 0.5. The algebra is identical; only the ROC changes the answer.

sections.h3: Residues, repeated poles and complex poles

blocks.text: The residue method sums residues of X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup> at the poles inside C. For a simple pole at z = p, the residue is lim<sub>z→p</sub> (z − p) X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup>.
x[n] = Σ Res[X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup> at poles inside C]
blocks.where: the sum runs over every pole of X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup> that lies inside the contour C.

blocks.text: For a pole of order m at z = p, use the repeated-pole formula: Res = (1/(m−1)!) lim<sub>z→p</sub> d<sup>m−1</sup>/dz<sup>m−1</sup> [(z − p)<sup>m</sup> X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup>]. Complex poles appear in conjugate pairs; combine them into a quadratic factor and use r<sup>n</sup>cos(ωn) and r<sup>n</sup>sin(ωn) pairs. Include a pole at z = 0 when it lies inside C; for n < 0 the factor z<sup>n−1</sup> is a negative power of z, so z = 0 becomes a pole of X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup> and adds a residue.

figure.caption: One pole produces two different sequences; the ROC alone selects which branch becomes the answer.

spec.title: Partial fractions with the ROC deciding the side
spec.aria: A downward flow from X(z) through partial fractions to one pole, which splits into two branches that end at the same output x[n].

examples.question: Find x[n] for X(z) = 1/((1 − 0.5z⁻¹)(1 − 2z⁻¹)) with ROC 0.5 < |z| < 2.
steps: Write X(z) = z²/[(z − 0.5)(z − 2)]. The poles are at z = 0.5 and z = 2.
The ROC has 0.5 < |z|, so the pole at 0.5 is right-sided: term is −(1/3)(0.5)ⁿu[n].
The ROC has |z| < 2, so the pole at 2 is left-sided: term is (4/3)(−2ⁿu[−n−1]) = −(4/3)(2)ⁿu[−n−1].
Add the two terms to get x[n].

traps: Using u[n] for every partial-fraction term out of habit. The same term gives a causal or an anti-causal sequence depending only on the ROC.
Dropping the minus sign on the left-sided pair: |z| < |a| gives −aⁿu[−n−1], not +aⁿu[−n−1].
Expanding in z⁻¹ when the ROC is |z| < r. That gives the right-sided coefficient sequence; left-sided needs expansion in positive powers of z.
Forgetting to include a pole at z = 0 in the residue sum when n < 0, because X(z) zⁿ⁻¹ can have a negative power of z.
Solving for A and B directly on X(z) instead of X(z)/z, which changes the coefficients and often leaves extra z factors in the answer.

quiz.q: State the contour-integral formula for the inverse Z-transform and define its symbols.
quiz.a: x[n] = (1/(2πj)) ∮<sub>C</sub> X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup> dz, where C is a closed counterclockwise contour inside the ROC, j = √(−1), n is the sample index, and X(z) is the z-transform.

quiz.q: Why can the same algebraic X(z) give two different sequences?
quiz.a: X(z) alone does not fix the sequence. The ROC fixes each pole's position relative to C: a pole inside the contour (|p| smaller than the radius of C, i.e. ROC |z| > |p|) gives the right-sided term pⁿu[n]; a pole outside it (ROC |z| < |p|) gives the left-sided term −pⁿu[−n−1]. Same partial fractions, different sequence.

quiz.q: Find x[n] for X(z) = 1/(1 − 0.8z⁻¹) with ROC |z| > 0.8.
quiz.a: The pole is at z = 0.8. ROC |z| > 0.8 makes the term right-sided, so x[n] = (0.8)ⁿu[n].

quiz.q: Find x[n] for X(z) = 1/(1 − 0.8z⁻¹) with ROC |z| < 0.8.
quiz.a: The pole is at z = 0.8. ROC |z| < 0.8 makes the term left-sided, so x[n] = −(0.8)ⁿu[−n−1].

quiz.q: A pole at z = 2 lies in the transform of a sequence whose ROC is 1 < |z| < 2. Is its inverse term right-sided or left-sided? Give the sequence.
quiz.a: The contour has radius less than 2, so the pole lies outside C. The term is left-sided: −2ⁿu[−n−1].

quiz.q: In the residue method for X(z) = 1/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹), why must z = 0 be checked when n < 0?
quiz.a: For n < 0, X(z) z<sup>n−1</sup> = z<sup>n</sup>/(z − 0.5) has a negative power of z, so z = 0 becomes a pole of order |n|. If it lies inside C its residue adds to x[n].

beyond: Not for the exam. Software such as MATLAB, SciPy and GNU Octave inverts a z-domain ratio by partial fractions or by evaluating the contour integral numerically. The same residue ideas return in the inverse Laplace transform and in digital-filter design. Search for inverse z-transform partial fractions, residue method, and symbolic z-transform inversion.
